articles.title: Singapore releases new emissions targets for 2035, on track to reaching net zero by 2050 - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: Singapore releases new emissions targets for 2035, on track to reaching net zero by 2050  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
Singapore on 10 February committed to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions to between 45 million and 50 million tonnes (Mt) by 2035, down from around 60 Mt in 2030.
This new climate target for 2035 puts Singapore on track to reach net zero emissions by 2050, with the planned decline in emissions on a linear trajectory.
Singapore’s new climate targets were submitted to the UN on 10 February, the official deadline for countries to submit their 2035 targets.
Of the almost 200 countries party to the Paris Agreement, the world’s climate pact, more than 10 have submitted their new pledges, including Britain, the US, Brazil, and the United Arab Emirates.
Singapore’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 were 58.59 Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2 eq). CO2 eq is a term used as a measurement of total greenhouse gases emitted. The Republic contributes about 0.1 per cent of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions.
“The lower bound of 45 Mt CO2 eq keeps us on a linear path to our net zero target in 2050, in line with international expectations,” said the National Climate Change Secretariat (NCCS) in a statement on 10 February.
“The range target (of 45 Mt to 50 Mt CO2 eq) takes into consideration the reality that as an alternative energy-disadvantaged island state, Singapore’s pace of decarbonisation depends heavily on developments in nascent mitigation technologies, and international collaboration,” NCCS added.

articles.title: When Climate Risk Becomes Economic Risk: The Philippines, ASEAN and a Changing World – Dr. Nirmal Ganguly - Mindanao Times
articles.summary: When Climate Risk Becomes Economic Risk: The Philippines, ASEAN and a Changing World – Dr. Nirmal Ganguly  Mindanao Times
articles.full_text:
CLIMATE change is usually discussed as an environmental problem. We hear about rising temperatures, stronger storms, changing rainfall, floods, droughts, and rising sea levels.
But for the Philippines, there is another way of looking at the same problem.
When a typhoon destroys a road, it is an infrastructure problem. When a flood closes a factory, it is a business problem. When drought damages a rice crop, it becomes a food and income problem. When a family loses its home, it becomes a household financial problem. When the government has to spend billions on reconstruction, it becomes a public-finance problem.
And when these things happen repeatedly, climate change becomes an economic problem.
That is why the climate debate in the Philippines needs to move beyond the environment. The real question is increasingly about how the country can protect its growth, jobs, incomes, infrastructure and development gains in a changing climate.
The real cost comes after the storm
The Philippines has no shortage of experience with natural disasters. But it is important to look beyond the immediate images of flooded streets, damaged houses and uprooted trees.
As of September 16, 2026, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council reported that damage to agriculture and infrastructure from tropical cyclones and the southwest monsoon since August had reached about ₱18.68 billion. Agricultural damage was estimated at ₱4.37 billion and infrastructure damage at ₱14.31 billion. The disasters had affected nearly 99,000 farmers and fisherfolk and damaged more than 81,000 hectares of crops.
Behind these numbers are real people.
A farmer may lose a harvest. A small shop may remain closed for several days. A worker may be unable to get to work. A family may have to borrow money to repair its home. A local government may have to divert money from another development project to repair a damaged road.
The cost of a disaster therefore does not end when the rain stops.
There is also the cost of lost production, lost income, lost working days and delayed investment.
That is the part of climate change that an economist needs to examine.
When a typhoon reaches the economy
Consider a simple example.
A bridge is damaged by a major storm. The government estimates the repair bill at ₱500 million.
That is the visible cost.
But suppose farmers on the other side of the bridge cannot bring their produce to market for several weeks. Workers cannot travel easily. Trucks have to take longer routes. Shops receive fewer customers. Food becomes more expensive.
The economic cost is now much larger than the repair bill.
This is why climate-related disasters can affect economic activity even when the physical damage appears relatively limited.
And if such disruptions happen again and again, the problem becomes more serious. Businesses may postpone investment. Families may reduce spending. Governments may have less money available for other development priorities.
Climate risk can gradually become a growth risk.
What happens to GDP?
There is an important distinction between recovering from a disaster and avoiding the economic consequences of repeated disasters.
An economy can rebuild after a typhoon. But rebuilding does not mean that the country has lost nothing.
If a newly built road has to be repaired repeatedly, resources that could have been used for a new school, hospital, irrigation system, or transport project are being used again to replace what was already built.
The World Bank Group’s Philippines Country Climate and Development Report, released on November 9, 2022, provides a sense of the potential scale of the problem. Its modeling estimated that climate-change damages could reduce the level of Philippine GDP by as much as 13.6% by 2040, relative to the relevant baseline, under the modeled climate-impact scenario. The report also estimated economic damages of up to 7.6% of GDP by 2030.
This does not mean that annual GDP growth would fall by 13.6%. It means that climate-related damage could leave the economy’s output level substantially below where it might otherwise have been.
That distinction matters.
The objective should not be to frighten people about the future. It should be to understand the economic cost of being unprepared.
Resilient infrastructure is not a luxury
This brings us to infrastructure.
When governments build roads, bridges, ports, electricity networks, water systems, schools and hospitals, they are making long-term investments.
But what happens if those investments are not designed with changing climate risks in mind?
The country may end up paying twice.
First, it pays to build the infrastructure.
Then it pays again to repair or replace it after a disaster.
There is therefore a strong economic argument for designing infrastructure to withstand the risks the country is increasingly likely to face.
An April 2026 Asian Development Bank assessment of the Laguna Lake area illustrates this broader approach. Laguna Lake supports more than 17 million people and important economic activities. The assessment emphasizes integrated, system-wide adaptation to safeguard livelihoods, ecosystems, and sustainable development.
The lesson extends beyond Laguna.
A flood-resistant road may cost more to build. A stronger drainage system may require greater initial investment. A power network designed to withstand extreme weather may be more expensive.
But the relevant question is not simply:
How much does resilience cost?
It is also:
-How much will the country lose if it does not invest in resilience?
That is a very different way of looking at development spending.
The farmer feels climate change first
For many ordinary Filipinos, the economic impact of climate change is felt not in GDP statistics but in the price of food.
Agriculture depends heavily on weather.
Too much rain can destroy crops. Too little rain can do the same. Extreme heat can reduce productivity. Floods can damage farmland, livestock, fishing and rural infrastructure.
On September 3, 2026, the Philippine Department of Agriculture reported that damage from heavy rains associated with the enhanced southwest monsoon and several tropical cyclones had reached ₱3.62 billion, affecting more than 86,000 farmers and fishers and more than 74,800 hectares of agricultural land.
The consequences do not stop with farmers.
When production falls, food supplies can tighten. Prices can rise. Families have to spend more on basic necessities. Poorer households are particularly vulnerable because food takes up a larger share of their household budgets.
This is how climate change travels from the farm to the kitchen table.
The next problem may be too little rain
There is another dimension that deserves attention.
The Philippines can move from dealing with excessive rainfall and flooding to worrying about drought.
On September 23, 2026, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, or PAGASA, warned that the ongoing Strong El Niño could intensify into a Very Strong El Niño between September and December 2026 and persist through the first half of 2027.
For farmers, this creates a difficult situation.
The problem is not simply that there is too much rain or too little rain.
It is that weather is becoming more difficult to predict and manage.
That uncertainty affects planting decisions, crop choices, farm investment and rural incomes.
It can also affect food prices and inflation.
The latest regional assessment reinforces this concern. In its September 2026 Asian Development Outlook, the Asian Development Bank identified a very strong El Niño as one of the principal risks to the region’s growth and inflation outlook. It warned that lower agricultural production and reduced hydropower could push food and energy prices higher.
Climate risk therefore enters the economy through one of the most basic things in everyday life: what people eat and what they pay for it.
Who pays when disaster strikes?
There is another question that deserves much greater attention:
Who ultimately pays for climate-related losses?
If a house, farm, shop or factory is insured, some of the financial burden can be transferred through insurance.
But many households and small businesses have limited insurance coverage.
When disaster strikes, they may have to use savings, borrow money or depend on government assistance.
The government then faces its own problem.
After a major disaster, it has to spend more on relief, reconstruction and social protection. Yet the same disaster may disrupt economic activity and reduce incomes and, potentially, government revenues.
A disaster can therefore become a fiscal shock.
This may sound like a technical financial issue.
It is not.
For an ordinary family, insurance can mean the difference between recovering and falling deeply into debt.
For government, better disaster-risk financing can mean preserving resources for schools, hospitals, infrastructure, and social protection instead of repeatedly diverting them toward emergency reconstruction.
Our cities cannot ignore the water
The economic importance of climate resilience becomes particularly visible in cities.
The Philippines is increasingly urban, and its major cities are centers of employment, commerce, manufacturing, services, transport, and investment.
When a major urban area floods, the damage goes far beyond flooded streets.
Workers cannot get to their jobs. Businesses close. Deliveries are delayed. Public transport is disrupted. Electricity and communications can be affected. Goods and equipment may be damaged.
A few hours of severe disruption can therefore affect thousands of businesses and large numbers of households.
For coastal cities, the challenge is even greater.
Flood management, drainage, land-use planning, building standards, transport systems and coastal protection need to be seen not simply as environmental measures but as economic infrastructure.

articles.title: Carbon Credits: The New Asset for Our Capital Markets - The Financial World
articles.summary: Carbon Credits: The New Asset for Our Capital Markets  The Financial World
articles.full_text:
Dr Aparna Mathur
India’s emerging carbon market could turn pollution reduction into a new financial opportunity for industry and investors
For decades, reducing carbon emissions was treated largely as an environmental obligation. That is changing rapidly. Carbon is increasingly acquiring a financial value, and the market emerging around it could become an important new component of the global financial system.
India, too, is preparing to enter this emerging market. Its Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) seeks to create a regulated framework under which companies that reduce their greenhouse-gas emissions can earn carbon credits, while those unable to meet prescribed emission targets can acquire credits to meet their obligations.
The development is significant not merely for environmental policy but also for India’s capital markets. If the system develops as envisaged, carbon credits could become a new class of tradable environmental assets, creating opportunities for businesses, financial institutions, technology companies, investors and a range of specialised service providers.
A carbon credit generally represents one metric tonne of carbon-dioxide equivalent whose emissions have been reduced, avoided or removed under an approved mechanism. The basic principle is straightforward: companies that reduce emissions beyond prescribed requirements can potentially generate credits, while companies facing compliance requirements can acquire them.
From environmental regulation to a market mechanism
The idea of putting a price on carbon is not new. Economists have long argued that market mechanisms can reduce pollution at lower overall compliance costs than relying exclusively on uniform regulatory requirements and penalties.
The concept received international recognition with the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which introduced three market-based mechanisms: International Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation. These mechanisms allowed countries and eligible entities to use emissions reductions and credits as part of their efforts to meet climate commitments.
The next major step came in 2005 with the launch of the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), one of the world’s largest carbon markets. It operates broadly on a “cap-and-trade” principle. A limit is placed on emissions from covered sectors, while companies receive or purchase allowances. Those that emit less than their permitted levels can sell surplus allowances, while those exceeding their limits need to acquire additional allowances or face penalties.
The experience of the EU helped demonstrate how environmental objectives could be linked with economic incentives. Carbon markets subsequently emerged in several jurisdictions, including California, New Zealand, South Korea and China.
India enters the carbon market
India’s carbon market is still at an early stage, but the creation of the CCTS represents an important shift in policy.
The objective is to establish a regulated mechanism for the generation, issuance and trading of Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs). Rather than viewing emission reduction simply as a cost imposed on industry, the emerging framework seeks to give it an economic value.
This could change the way Indian companies approach decarbonisation. Investment in energy efficiency, renewable energy, cleaner production processes, waste management and other emission-reduction activities could potentially create an additional financial return through carbon credits.
For businesses, therefore, reducing emissions may increasingly become both an environmental responsibility and an economic strategy.
Who could benefit?
The impact of a functioning carbon market could extend well beyond large industrial companies.
Cement, steel and aluminium companies, among other energy-intensive industries, could benefit from adopting cleaner production technologies and reducing their dependence on high-carbon fuels.
Renewable-energy companies involved in solar, wind and biomass projects could potentially generate carbon credits where their projects meet the applicable requirements and emission reductions are independently verified.
Waste-management companies represent another potential area of opportunity. Better management of landfill waste can reduce methane emissions, while rehabilitation of existing landfills and conversion of waste into useful resources can create environmental as well as economic benefits.
Forestry and nature-based projects could also participate where they can demonstrate measurable and verifiable carbon absorption or removal.
The emerging market could create opportunities for technology companies developing digital systems to measure, monitor and manage emissions. Companies specialising in carbon projects could identify and develop ventures capable of generating eligible credits.
There could also be growing demand for consultants and independent verification agencies. Their role would be particularly important because the credibility of a carbon market depends on accurate measurement and verification of claimed emission reductions.
Building the regulatory architecture
A carbon market cannot function effectively without a credible institutional framework. India’s CCTS therefore involves several government and regulatory bodies.
The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) has a central role in administering and developing the Indian carbon market. Its responsibilities include identifying sectors with emission-reduction potential, establishing requirements and procedures, accrediting verification agencies and overseeing the processes associated with carbon-credit certificates.
The Grid Controller of India (Grid-India) operates the Indian Carbon Market Registry, which maintains digital records of participating entities and their carbon-credit holdings and transactions.
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) has a regulatory role in the trading of carbon credits. It oversees the relevant trading framework and approves business rules for power exchanges involved in carbon-credit trading.
Independent Accredited Carbon Verification Agencies (ACVAs) are another critical element. They are expected to verify whether claimed emission reductions have actually occurred and whether projects meet prescribed standards. Without credible verification, the market could face problems of inaccurate claims or low-quality credits.
The National Steering Committee for Indian Carbon Market (NSCICM) provides another layer of institutional oversight and makes recommendations concerning market procedures, emission targets, issuance of credits and related rules.
A new opportunity—but also a test of credibility
For India’s financial ecosystem, carbon credits could eventually become more than instruments for regulatory compliance. Their tradability creates the possibility of a new environmental asset class linked to the transition towards a low-carbon economy.
But the success of the market will depend heavily on its credibility. Carbon credits must represent genuine and measurable emission reductions. Transparent measurement, reliable data, independent verification and clear trading rules will be essential.
There is also a broader economic opportunity. A functioning carbon market can encourage investment in cleaner technologies, renewable energy, energy efficiency, circular-economy solutions and innovative waste-management systems. It can create demand for new financial, technological and professional services while encouraging industries to factor the cost of carbon into business decisions.
India has set a goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070. The carbon market will not, by itself, deliver that objective. But by attaching an economic value to emission reduction, it can potentially align environmental objectives with commercial incentives.
The transition from a system in which carbon reduction is primarily a regulatory obligation to one in which it also carries a market value marks an important development. If India can build a transparent, well-regulated and credible carbon market, carbon credits could emerge as a significant instrument of sustainable finance—and potentially as a new frontier for India’s capital markets.
Dr Aparna Mathur teaches financial management at Christ University, Ghaziabad

articles.full_text:
Diginex Launches Supply Chain Due Diligence Platform for $7 Billion Market
- Diginex has launched an enhanced supply chain due diligence platform as the sustainability software market is forecast to exceed $7 billion by 2029.
- The platform maps suppliers across multiple tiers and combines company, worker and third-party data to identify risks and track corrective actions.
- Regulatory pressure is increasing as the EU prepares to enforce new due diligence requirements and a forced labour product ban from December 2027.
Diginex has launched an enhanced end-to-end supply chain due diligence platform as companies face mounting pressure to identify environmental, social and compliance risks beyond their direct suppliers.
The platform gives companies a continuous view of risks, actions and outcomes across multiple tiers of their supply chains. Diginex said the system is designed to replace fragmented supplier information and manual processes with verified, traceable data.
The launch targets a rapidly expanding market. Verdantix forecasts the global supply chain sustainability software sector will grow at a 29% compound annual rate through 2029. The market is expected to exceed $7 billion by then.
Regulation pushes due diligence deeper into supply chains
Companies are facing greater expectations to understand where risks sit across increasingly complex supplier networks.
Regulation is also moving beyond corporate disclosure. New rules increasingly require companies to demonstrate how they identify, assess and respond to risks within their value chains.
In Europe, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive has increased the focus on corporate responsibility for supply chain impacts. The EU Forced Labour Regulation adds another layer of scrutiny.
From December 2027, the regulation will prohibit products made with forced labour from being placed on or exported from the EU market.
For companies operating global supply chains, this raises the importance of reliable supplier data and documented remediation processes. Businesses may need evidence not only that a risk was identified, but also what they did about it.
“Regulation increasingly requires businesses to build a more complete picture of risk across their supply chains. That requires more than visibility, it requires actionable data that helps companies understand where risks sit, determine where to act and measure the outcomes,” said Archana Kotecha, Interim Chief Executive Officer of Diginex. “Our solution is designed to connect those dots, helping businesses move from risk identification to action and measurable outcomes.”
From supplier mapping to verified remediation
Diginex has structured the platform around four stages of supply chain due diligence.
Companies can first map suppliers across multiple tiers. They can then identify and validate potential risks by comparing company-reported information with worker-reported and third-party data.
Once a risk is identified, companies can manage corrective action plans with suppliers through the platform. The system then maintains a traceable record from the initial finding through to verified resolution.
This approach addresses a persistent challenge for multinational companies. Supply chain information often sits across procurement systems, spreadsheets, supplier questionnaires and third-party databases. That fragmentation can make it difficult to establish a consistent record of due diligence.

Diginex said centralising that information can also provide benefits beyond regulatory compliance.
The company expects the platform to help lower operating costs by reducing fragmented data management. A documented, evidence-based due diligence process could also help companies manage litigation exposure.
Clearer accountability may support supplier and worker retention as well, particularly where companies use remediation rather than supplier termination as their primary response to identified risks.
Diginex plans to extend the platform over time, subject to customer research and prioritisation.
Supply chain data becomes a governance issue
For corporate leaders, the growth of supply chain due diligence regulation is turning supplier visibility into a broader governance and risk-management issue.
Procurement teams increasingly need to coordinate with legal, sustainability, compliance and executive leadership. Investors may also seek clearer evidence of how companies identify and manage human rights and sustainability risks beyond their direct operations.
The projected growth of the sustainability software market reflects that shift. As regulatory requirements expand, companies will need systems capable of producing defensible evidence rather than simply collecting supplier disclosures.
For businesses exposed to European and other regulated markets, the challenge is moving from knowing who sits within the supply chain to demonstrating what happens when risks emerge. With new rules approaching implementation, that distinction is becoming increasingly important for compliance, governance and operational resilience.

articles.title: Formula E Achieves 241% Social Impact Boost in Net Zero Plan - sustainabilitymag.com
articles.summary: Formula E Achieves 241% Social Impact Boost in Net Zero Plan  sustainabilitymag.com
articles.full_text:
Formula E reports a 241% year-over-year increase in social impact and a certified shift from carbon neutrality to a science-based net-zero approach.
Using a new impact framework developed with Deloitte, Formula E contributed an estimated €5.6m (US$6.3m) in social value across race locations, achieving a Social Return on Investment (SROI) ratio of 2.7. The championship reported the findings in its 2024/25 Season Sustainability Report.
The 2024/25 Season saw a shift across the championship's strategic pillars: Formula Excellence, Formula Equity, Formula Environment and Formula Ecosystem. Formula E integrated sustainability into procurement, contracts and daily operations.
"Our mission has always been about accelerating progress," says Julia Pallé, VP Sustainability at Formula E.
"While carbon calculation is grounded in direct physical measurements, quantifying human impact requires a different set of tools.
“In Season 11, we set out to bring that same standard of accountability to our social footprint, working with Deloitte to build an evidence-based framework to measure our work.
“Reaching over 86,000 people and delivering an estimated €5.6m (US$6.3m) in social value contribution demonstrates the tangible difference sport can make in host communities."
Key sustainability milestones achieved
Formula E monitored key performance metrics across its environmental, social and economic initiatives:
- Achieved certification under the BSI Net Zero Pathway following an independent audit, becoming the first sport globally to align with ISO 14064 and IWA 42 guidelines.
- Reduced overall greenhouse gas emissions by 18% compared to both the 2023/24 Season and the 2018 baseline
- Decreased freight-related carbon emissions by 28% year-over-year by reducing air freight cargo planes and increasing use of sea, road and rail transport.
- Generated €187m (US$210m) in Gross Value Added across host cities, supporting 4,300 jobs, including an estimated 680 sustainability-focused roles based on OECD benchmarks.
- Hosted the first all-women test session in FIA World Championship history in November 2024, featuring 17 drivers in the GEN3 Evo car and creating three permanent positions within the ecosystem.
Climate governance and decarbonisation framework
The organisation's verified Net Zero Pathway sets near-term targets to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50% and Scope 3 emissions by 27.5% by 2030.
Long-term plans aim for a 90% absolute reduction across Scopes 1, 2 and 3 by 2050.
In the 2024/25 Season, all race locations used 100% renewable energy by prioritising grid connections and using Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO) biofuels in temporary generators, along with solar power and battery storage.
Operational emissions decreased by 20% to 1,204 CO2e supported by expanded remote production.
Meanwhile, residual emissions were offset by retiring Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) from the Inner Mongolia Wujier Phase I Wind Power Project and the Core Carbon Principles-labelled Brusque Landfill Gas Project in Brazil.
“Our mission has always been about accelerating progress ”Julia PalléVP Sustainability, Formula E
Equity, diversity and social impact
Formula E’s social impact strategy was guided by the launch of its Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Strategy for 2025–2027. The corporate workforce comprised 54.9% females, 19.9% ethnic minorities and 21% working-class representation.
The Better Futures Fund expanded from a pilot to a championship-wide programme, allocating €250,000 (US$280,000) across ten host cities to support more than 8,000 beneficiaries.
Local partners included the Change Please Foundation's ULEZ mobile care buses in London, sensory rooms at the First Autism Centre in Jeddah and refugee inclusion initiatives at Berlin Tempelhof.
The FIA Girls on Track initiative engaged 1,272 young women across race markets. Additionally, Formula E launched the Diversity in Motorsport Fund and a research initiative to identify barriers for women in elite racing.
Key partners
Google Cloud
Google Cloud is a strategic technology partner, allowing Formula E to replace carbon-intensive on-site computing hardware with cloud infrastructure. Using data centres with a fleet-wide Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.09, Formula E processes telemetry and race data efficiently and scales server capacity dynamically during race weekends to avoid idle energy consumption.
DHL
As Formula E’s official logistics partner, DHL collaborated with championship teams to audit global freight movements and reduce air freight volume by 80 tonnes. By duplicating essential track equipment into ocean freight kits and optimising transport routes by sea, road, and rail, the initiative eliminated one cargo aircraft for non-European races, saving about 5,000 tonnes of carbon emissions.
Infosys
Infosys works with Formula E to deploy digital technologies and artificial intelligence across its Scope 3 emissions value chain. The platform streamlines data management, automates reporting for audit readiness, and uses predictive analytics to model emissions scenarios across global supply chains, logistics, and procurement.

articles.title: Circular Economy Act must strengthen EU’s EPR framework, say industry voices - Packaging Europe
articles.summary: Circular Economy Act must strengthen EU’s EPR framework, say industry voices  Packaging Europe
articles.full_text:
EUROPEN is one of 40+ industry associations calling for a stronger Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework under the Circular Economy Act – setting their sights on a functioning European market for secondary raw materials.
In a joint statement, the signatories describe the Circular Economy Act as a ‘unique opportunity’ to develop a strong market for secondary raw materials in the EU and strengthen Europe’s circular economy.
They urge policymakers to develop a ‘more harmonized and enforceable’ framework to tackle fragmentation between national systems – allowing materials to circulate across Member State borders, supporting investment in recycling infrastructure, and boosting the continent’s competitiveness and strategic autonomy.
The statement sets out six priorities for the Circular Economy Act, including a directly applicable EU EPR Regulation based on Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. This is expected to reduce fragmentation, align national rules, and unlock a functioning market for secondary raw materials.
Another priority is producer-led EPR governance. According to the statement, producers should retain decision-making responsibility, alongside EPR fees dedicated to waste management.
Furthermore, the organizations call for the Circular Economy Act to establish transparent reporting across the waste chain and mandate standardized, comparable data – a move anticipated to increase accountability and pave the way for more performance-based EPR systems.
EPR funds should be earmarked for the waste streams they finance and directed to the infrastructure required to meet the EU’s recycling targets, the signatories say.
The statement also encourages policymakers to reduce administrative complexity by removing ‘unnecessary’ requirements and harmonizing EPR registration. This is anticipated to reduce barriers to cross-border compliance, especially for SMEs and micro-enterprises.
Additionally, the signatories believe that separate collection infrastructure should be improved, with more public awareness set to achieve reliable waste streams and improve recycling rates.
Altogether, the signatories aspire to introduce the necessary systems, investments, and market conditions to ensure that materials are collected, recycled, and re-circulated at scale across the continent.
“At a time when there is growing momentum to complete Europe’s Single Market, the Circular Economy Act is a unique opportunity to build a strong market for secondary raw materials,” says Sévrine Pereira Teixeira, senior public affairs manager at EUROPEN.
“The fragmentation of EPR systems creates barriers to cross-border activities, deters investment in recycling capacity and ultimately holds back the development of a truly European circular economy.
“Europe needs a harmonized and enforceable framework that unlocks investment in recycling and strengthens Europe’s competitiveness and strategic autonomy."
Earlier this year, EUROPEN commissioned a study arguing that the Circular Economy Act must address ‘wide’ performance gaps between national packaging EPR systems across the EU. The study warns that targets alone will not unlock circularity across the bloc, and that investment in collection, sorting and recycling systems is also required.
EUROPEN has also advocated for a digital One-Stop Shop to be introduced for EU-wide EPR implementation under the Circular Economy Act. A single ‘point of entry’ for all mandated EPR schemes is anticipated to ease administrative burdens on companies and authorities alike.

articles.summary: French regulator asks EU to strengthen PAI and transition plan rules in SFDR 2.0  Investment & Pensions Europe
articles.full_text:
The Autorité des Marchés Financiers (AMF) has made a slew of recommendations to strengthen the credibility of the next iteration of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR).
The French financial regulator published a report on Thursday laying out the views of a working group which includes representatives from many of the country’s banks, asset managers, NGOs, universities and government departments.
The document focuses on two of the most controversial proposals on the table for SFDR 2.0: the inclusion of a category for ‘transition’ assets, and the introduction of a more flexible approach to disclosing the negative environmental and social impacts of a fund (known as PAIs).
On the former, the European Commission wants “credible” transition plans to be one method for investors seeking to demonstrate their assets or portfolios qualify for the proposed Article 7 category.
But AMF’s working group agreed that the term “credible” was too loose and legally ambiguous.
“It should be accompanied by explicit common minimum criteria and refer to an associated framework or standard,” it recommended.
“Credibility implies evidence: it can only be assessed against a recognised authority or standard. It is essential, first and foremost, to define the criteria for this ‘credibility’, and a change of terminology to require a ‘robust’, ‘coherent’ or ‘high-quality’ transition plan would not resolve the fundamental issues.”
Specifically, the group recommends that a credible transition plan should be based on a “recognised framework regarding compatibility with the Paris Agreement”, include clear decarbonisation targets – including Scope 3 goals – and be able to point to past efforts to cut emissions.
“The past trajectory and future targets must be directly linked to the measures put in place and planned, and supported by concrete evidence,” it continued, pointing to existing financing efforts and the incorporation of targets into governance measures.
The report suggests that issuers could disclose the proportion of capital expenditure they allocate to polluting activities, so that stakeholders can assess how aligned the stated transition commitments are with actual business decisions.
PAIs
AMF’s working group also made a series of recommendations about the future of PAIs within SFDR. The Commission has proposed mandatory disclosure of PAIs for ‘sustainable’ and transition’ portfolios, and promised to create a list of credible indicators once the legislation has been agreed.
European Parliament, on the other hand, looks set to push for a more complex regime combining mandatory and voluntary PAIs.
The report supported the Commission’s approach, but recommended “rethinking the indicators as a whole rather than simply ‘cherry-picking’ from the current list”.
It said portfolios with a significant allocation to carbon-intensive assets should have to disclose “mandatory sector-specific PAIs”.
AMF’s report, which was developed between March and June this year, has been approved by its board.

articles.title: Exclusive: Radisson’s net zero hero - hotelmanagement.com.au
articles.summary: Exclusive: Radisson’s net zero hero  hotelmanagement.com.au
articles.full_text:
In an interview with Radisson Hotel Group’s Jens Brandin, he delves into why Manchester became a test case for verified net zero. Tristan Rayner reports.
This article first appeared in HM Magazine’s June issue; read it online here.
The relaunch of Radisson’s Manchester city centre property was a refurbishment and rebrand, while also serving as a live test of whether a lower-carbon hotel model can work for owners, for travellers, for corporates, and for the long term. Jens Brandin, Cluster General Manager at RHG, dives deep into what it means after a year of real data as RHG expands the mission.
When Radisson Hotel Group reopened its Manchester city centre property as a verified net zero hotel, it was not a brand exercise. For Jens Brandin, Cluster General Manager, it was simpler and harder than that: could you actually run a lower-carbon hotel and have the numbers make sense?
Brandin has been with Radisson since 1999, starting in Berlin and working across Europe and Africa in the years since. In conversation about the Manchester hotel, he doesn’t talk about sustainability abstractions but about the actual decisions around heat pumps, electricity costs, menu changes, supplier negotiations, and what you can put in front of an owner on a P&L.
The property, which had been operating as a Park Inn, was repositioned under the Radisson brand alongside a renovation worth some £4 million to £5 million, or somewhere around AUD$10 million at the time. Doing both at once wasn’t just convenient, but served as the point.
As Brandin explains, major infrastructure decisions in hotels play out over 20-year cycles. And if the industry is going to understand what net zero costs and what it delivers, someone has to go first.
“Whatever milestone year people are working toward, the investment cycle for major hotel infrastructure can be up to 20 years,” he said. “That means the industry needs to be testing and proving these models now. If we wait too long, we miss the window to make meaningful changes.”
RHG’s leased portfolio, where the operator controls energy purchasing and building decisions directly, made Manchester a practical choice for that kind of test. But Brandin is clear about why the exercise mattered beyond the asset in what may become England’s second city, judging by the cranes and high-rise in the city.
“This project is so important because we need to be able to show owners, within a one-year P&L, what happens when you make these investments,” he said.
The hotel carries a “Verified Net Zero” designation (or VNZ), which appears on both on RHG’s own sites but also booking sites, where potential guests see it as they search for a suitable stay in Manchester.
Brandin is careful to explain VNZ rather than oversell: under the definitions, Scope 1 and 2 emissions are those that have been addressed directly; the remaining verified footprint is offset through a UK carbon capture agriculture program. TÜV Rheinland independently verified the result, one of the most trusted brands in Europe.
That leaves Scope 3 emissions, which include the supply chain, food and beverage, the outsourced laundry service — and this is a different challenge entirely.
“Scope 3 is really the most difficult part, because we cannot solve that by ourselves,” he said. “The supply chain has to move with us, whether that is laundry, suppliers, or food and beverage.”
Again, he isn’t soft on being realistic there on timelines.
“I think fully net zero, without carbon offsets, will take at least another 20 years,” he said.
It’s a refreshing insight from one of the insiders within RHG’s flagship sustainability project. Brandin compares the trajectory to free-range eggs; niche and expensive until enough buyers pushed the whole supply chain to shift.
“The more businesses ask for these products, the more suppliers will offer them,” he said.
The commercial pressure is already visible in the RFP process. Corporate clients are increasingly including sustainability criteria as part of procurement decisions either by choice or through compliance, and Brandin said that is not going away regardless of how the broader public conversation around climate shifts.
“Even when the public conversation changes, there is still a strong underlying expectation that businesses should reduce their environmental impact,” he said. “People may not always talk about it loudly, but the demand is there and it continues to shape decision-making.”
Brandin indicated early performance from Manchester is holding up, with guest awareness of the VNZ designation as tracking above 70 per cent, with around one in five guests indicating it directly influenced their booking decision.
There is also a workforce argument that can be overlooked. For a hotel in the UK, in a post-Brexit, post-Covid environment where hospitality recruitment has been a persistent pressure, Brandin says a “highly credible sustainability proposition can help a property compete for staff as well as bookings.”
On the numbers: May 2026 will mark a full year of trading data for the hotel in its current configuration. Brandin said the model is currently costing “a little bit more than a normal hotel”, but not dramatically so. The bigger operational challenge has been the heat pump.
“The biggest challenge at the moment is electricity,” he said, gesturing to the rooftop where the large heat pumps are installed. “We have a relatively new prototype heat pump, and the supplier is learning with us, so the savings are not coming through as quickly as we originally assumed.”
That kind of specific, useful detail is where Brandin shines, detailing the nuts and bolts of how sustainability announcements are maintained in the day-to-day operation of the hotel.
Within the hotel rooms themselves, there are few indications that anything is operating differently. Core comforts remain indistinguishable in the form of modern showers and large smart TVs. Instead, there are quiet removals of plastic water bottles, replaced by refillable glass carafes, and menus and hotel info are QR-code or app-based, while amenities can be requested rather than provided by default.
PILOT BECOMES A KEY PROGRAMME
Manchester was joined by Oslo’s Radisson RED in 2025 as its two Verified Net Zero properties across RHG’s portfolio of some 1,520 hotels in operation and under development. While at the time of the interview Brandin could only hint at more to come, the group made its next step with its VNZ ambitions on March 23 at the International Hospitality Investment Forum in Berlin.
At the Forum, RHG announced it is scaling its Verified Net Zero program from pilot into a multi-year rollout, starting with 10 more VNZ properties in 2026, and targeting 100 properties by 2030. The company said its 2026 expansion begins in Norway and the UK before moving into Denmark, Sweden and South Africa. Germany, Austria and Spain’s Canary Islands were also referenced as markets in the five-year pipeline.
Inge Huijbrechts, RHG’s Chief Sustainability and Security Officer, said the results gave the group the confidence to move from proof-of-concept to program.
“The hotels show strong carbon reduction across all emission scopes, high guest awareness, and clear support for sustainable meetings and events,” she said. “They also provide hotel owners with a practical pathway to future-proof their properties.”
For asset owners who are interested but will want to keenly be aware of the capital expenditure, Huijbrechts told this publication that the investment case extends well beyond sustainability credentials, listing fossil fuel price volatility, tightening EU green building regulation and growing investor appetite for ESG-credentialled assets are all converging.
Huijbrechts noted that research from CBRE found that 79 per cent of European institutional investors said they would pay a premium for assets with strong ESG credentials, a figure the group is able to put in front of franchised and managed hotel owners as it builds out the program.
Back in Manchester, Brandin hinted that an expansion would validate the approach, and the decision to start before anyone was entirely sure how it would go.
“We had to start somewhere,” he said.

Türkiye is preparing a major push to cut emissions from heavy industry, backed by $250 million in catalytic funding from the Climate Investment Funds (CIF). CIF’s governing board endorsed the […]

articles.full_text:
CIF Backs Türkiye’s Industrial Decarbonization With $250 Million, Mobilizing $2.8 Billion
- Climate Investment Funds has approved $250 million in catalytic funding for Türkiye, expected to mobilize $2.8 billion in total investment.
- The program targets 39 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in annual avoided or reduced emissions by 2035, supporting Türkiye’s 2053 net-zero goal.
- Green finance could reach 378 businesses by 2035, with SMEs and women-led enterprises among the priorities.
Türkiye is preparing a major push to cut emissions from heavy industry, backed by $250 million in catalytic funding from the Climate Investment Funds (CIF).
CIF’s governing board endorsed the financing package as Türkiye works to accelerate investment in cleaner industrial production. The plan is expected to mobilize $2.8 billion in total capital.
Of that amount, $1.93 billion is expected from CIF’s multilateral development bank partners. A further $870 million is expected from private investors and other sources.
The program will target some of the most difficult areas of industrial decarbonization. These include green hydrogen, carbon capture, utilization and storage, energy efficiency and circular economy initiatives.
Funding will also support renewable electricity deployment, climate technologies and the development of green markets.
Industrial emissions move to the center of Türkiye’s climate strategy
The investment plan is projected to reduce or avoid 39 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually by 2035.
That reduction would support Türkiye’s longer-term goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2053. It also comes as industrial emissions face greater scrutiny from policymakers, investors and international trading partners.
The Ministry of Treasury and Finance and Ministry of Industry and Technology developed the plan. It aligns with Türkiye’s 2025 Climate Law and the country’s pilot national Emissions Trading System.
Implementation will run through multilateral development bank partners and the Türkiye Industrial Decarbonization Investment Platform, known as TIDIP.
The platform has a broader target of mobilizing up to approximately $5.77 billion for industrial decarbonization by 2030.
RELATED ARTICLE: CIF Launches $1 Billion Industry Decarbonization Drive with Seven Emerging Economies
Concessional finance targets early-stage technology risk
CIF expects its anchor capital to mobilize more than $11 in investment for every dollar it deploys under the plan.
The Asian Development Bank, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and World Bank Group, including IFC, will deliver CIF funding through the platform.
The structure pairs concessional finance with MDB balance sheets, technical expertise and private capital.
That approach addresses a persistent financing challenge for industrial decarbonization. Technologies such as green hydrogen and CCUS often require substantial upfront capital. Investors can also face technology, market and infrastructure risks that remain difficult to price commercially.
CIF’s Industry Decarbonization investment program is designed specifically to address those barriers in developing economies.
The initiative uses concessional capital to absorb early-stage risks and attract commercial investment into emerging technologies and markets. It also includes a 50% to 100% private-sector financing carve-out at project level.
Seven inaugural countries have been selected for the program. Brazil, Mexico and Türkiye have each secured endorsements of $250 million.
SMEs and green jobs enter the investment equation
Türkiye also intends to use the funding to expand access to green finance across its industrial base.
An estimated 378 businesses could gain improved access by 2035. The program will place particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises and women-led businesses.
Just transition measures, gender equality and social inclusion are also embedded in the investment plan. The aim is to ensure industrial restructuring creates opportunities for workers and communities affected by the move away from carbon-intensive production.
For corporate leaders and investors, the program adds another layer to Türkiye’s changing industrial landscape. Climate regulation, emissions pricing and access to concessional capital are increasingly intersecting with decisions about technology and competitiveness.
The $2.8 billion financing plan could provide an early test of whether blended finance can move capital into industrial technologies at meaningful scale.
Its wider relevance extends beyond Türkiye. Heavy industry remains among the hardest parts of the global economy to decarbonize. Mobilizing private investment alongside public and concessional capital will be central to determining how quickly emerging economies can make that transition.

articles.title: Garanti BBVA Raises $125 Million to Finance Green SMEs
articles.summary:
Garanti BBVA has completed a $125 million sustainable subordinated bond issuance with a consortium comprising IFC and DEG. The transaction will strengthen the Turkish bank’s capital structure while directing financing […]
The post Garanti BBVA Raises $125 Million to Finance Green SMEs appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Garanti BBVA Raises $125 Million to Finance Green SMEs
- Garanti BBVA has completed a $125 million sustainable Tier II bond issuance with IFC and DEG, strengthening its regulatory capital base.
- Proceeds will finance electric vehicles, energy-efficient technologies and other green investments by micro-enterprises and SMEs in Türkiye.
- The transaction will also expand access to finance for women entrepreneurs, combining capital strengthening with sustainable and inclusive lending.
Garanti BBVA has completed a $125 million sustainable subordinated bond issuance with a consortium comprising IFC and DEG. The transaction will strengthen the Turkish bank’s capital structure while directing financing toward green investments and women entrepreneurs.
The 10-year Tier II bond includes a call option exercisable from the fifth year. It also brings Garanti BBVA back to the subordinated bond market after several years.
For the bank, the structure serves two purposes. It adds regulatory capital and provides funding that can reach businesses facing the costs of the green transition.
Capital Meets the Real Economy
Garanti BBVA plans to channel proceeds toward eligible green and social investments under its sustainable finance framework.
On the environmental side, financing will target micro-enterprises and SMEs investing in electric vehicles, energy-efficient equipment and technologies, and other eligible green projects. These businesses often face capital constraints when upgrading equipment or reducing their environmental footprint.
The social component will focus on improving women entrepreneurs’ access to finance.
The transaction also broadens Garanti BBVA’s relationships with international financial institutions and diversifies its capital funding channels.
Atıl Özus, Executive Vice President for Finance and Treasury at Garanti BBVA, said: “We consider our longstanding partnerships with international financial institutions important not only for strengthening our Bank’s funding structure, but also for developing new financing models that respond to the needs of the real economy.” “By supporting our regulatory capital base, this issuance allows us to further diversify our relationships with international institutions and our capital funding channels.”
Sustainable Finance Targets SME Transition
The bond places smaller businesses at the centre of the bank’s sustainable finance strategy. For many SMEs, decarbonisation requires upfront investment in vehicles, equipment and technology before efficiency gains can be realised.
Sinem Edige, Executive Vice President at Garanti BBVA, said: “We see sustainable finance as a key element of our long-term strategy and an important contributor to financing the economic transition. We will use the funding provided through this transaction to support the green transition investments of micro-enterprises and SMEs and access to finance for women entrepreneurs.”
Edige said the bank views sustainability as extending beyond individual financial products. Garanti BBVA intends to combine financing with advisory services and other solutions as customers navigate their transition plans.
The issuance comes as parent group BBVA participates in COP31 as Global Banking Partner, placing the transaction within a broader international climate finance agenda.
RELATED ARTICLE: Garanti BBVA Issues $34M Green Bond for Agriculture
IFC and DEG Back Inclusive Growth
The participation of IFC and DEG brings development finance institutions into the bank’s regulatory capital structure while connecting their investment to measurable economic priorities.
Momina Aijazuddin, Director of the Financial Institutions Group for the Middle East, Central Asia and Türkiye at IFC, said: “This investment builds on IFC’s longstanding and impactful partnership with Garanti BBVA and reflects our shared commitment to sustainable and inclusive growth in Türkiye.” By strengthening Garanti BBVA’s capacity to finance micro, small, and medium enterprises, we are helping expand opportunities for women entrepreneurs while supporting businesses investing in the energy transition—helping them grow more sustainably, strengthen their competitiveness, and contribute to Türkiye’s energy transition.”
Gudrun Busch, Senior Director for Financial Institutions and Capital Markets at DEG, said: “Our joint investment strengthens the Bank’s capitalization and supports financing for green MSME projects and women entrepreneurs.”
Why It Matters for Investors and Executives
The issuance shows how banks can use capital instruments to support both balance-sheet resilience and transition finance. That structure is particularly relevant in emerging markets, where SMEs account for significant economic activity but can struggle to fund cleaner technologies.
For executives, access to dedicated green finance can lower one barrier to investing in efficiency and electrification. For investors, the transaction illustrates how international development capital can support bank resilience while directing financing toward environmental and social objectives.
For Türkiye, the wider significance lies in whether transactions of this kind can translate institutional capital into investment across the real economy. Expanding that channel will be important as businesses face growing pressure to improve efficiency, competitiveness and readiness for a lower-carbon global economy.

articles.full_text:
EY Appoints Jennifer Leitsch as Americas Community Impact and Sustainability Leader
- Jennifer Leitsch has been appointed EY Americas Community Impact and Sustainability Leader and Executive Director of the Ernst & Young Foundation.
- The expanded role brings EY’s corporate sustainability work closer to its social impact, education and workforce initiatives.
- Leitsch moves into the position after two years leading EY’s corporate sustainability efforts in the US, alongside senior client advisory work in climate and sustainability.
Jennifer Leitsch is taking on an expanded leadership role at EY, combining oversight of the firm’s Americas sustainability agenda with community impact and the Ernst & Young Foundation.
Leitsch has been appointed EY Americas Community Impact and Sustainability Leader and Executive Director of the Ernst & Young Foundation. The move broadens her responsibilities beyond the corporate sustainability work she has led for the past two years.
The appointment places environmental strategy, community investment and workforce development within a more connected leadership structure. It also brings together several programs that touch employees, universities and communities across EY’s Americas operations.
Sustainability and social impact come together
Leitsch announced the transition on LinkedIn, describing the expanded mandate as an opportunity to connect several areas of EY’s impact strategy.
“I’m excited to share that I’m stepping into an expanded role as EY Americas Community Impact and Sustainability Leader and Executive Director of the Ernst & Young Foundation. I take on these new responsibilities with tremendous gratitude for Ellen Glazerman, whose leadership and commitment have shaped an exceptional team and a powerful legacy. I am honored to build on that foundation and wish Ellen the very best in retirement.”
Leitsch succeeds Ellen Glazerman as she retires and will build on an established portfolio of community and education programs.
Her new remit brings together corporate sustainability with EY Ripples, the Ernst & Young Foundation, University Relations and the EY Academic Resource Center. The structure creates closer links between environmental priorities and programs focused on communities, education and the future workforce.
For large professional services firms, that integration has become increasingly relevant. Sustainability functions now intersect with talent, governance, reporting, procurement and corporate citizenship. Companies are also facing greater scrutiny over how sustainability commitments translate into operational decisions and measurable outcomes.
Experience spanning corporate strategy and client advisory
Leitsch brings more than 17 years of sustainability experience to the expanded position. Her background includes sustainability strategy, programs and reporting, with 12 years spent working across two global corporations.
As EY Americas Corporate Sustainability Leader, she has led the firm’s internal sustainability strategy and reporting in the US.
She has also served as a managing director in Ernst & Young LLP’s Climate Change and Sustainability Services practice. There, she has worked with clients to develop and advance sustainability strategies.
RELATED ARTICLE: EY Launches Framework to Put Financial Value on Sustainability Risks
Leitsch reflected on those relationships as she announced the transition.
“As I make this transition, I’m also deeply grateful to my colleagues in our Climate Change and Sustainability Services practice. The relationships I’ve built and the experiences we’ve shared have meant so much to me, both personally and professionally.”
Her experience across internal corporate sustainability and external advisory work gives the expanded role a broad remit. It connects the operational challenges companies face internally with the sustainability expectations EY encounters through its client work.
Governance and the future workforce
Education and governance have also formed a significant part of Leitsch’s work.
She serves on the Board of Advisors and Sustainable Business Advisory Council at the University of Colorado Denver Business School. She also established the Jennifer Leitsch Endowed Scholarship Fund for graduate students studying sustainable business.
Leitsch developed and teaches Accounting and Finance for Sustainability, a graduate-level elective offered twice each year.
She also serves as board secretary and chair of the Nominating and Governance Committee for the United Nations Global Compact Network USA.
Her expanded EY role now provides a platform to connect these areas more directly with the firm’s sustainability and community programs.
“After leading our corporate sustainability efforts for the past two years, I’m energized by the opportunity to bring that work together with our social impact efforts through EY Ripples, the Ernst & Young Foundation, University Relations, and the EY Academic Resource Center. Most of all, I’m excited to work alongside and learn from the talented team that brings this work to life every day. Together, we have an incredible opportunity to strengthen our impact on our people, our communities, the environment and the future workforce.”
For executives and sustainability leaders, the appointment reflects the widening scope of corporate sustainability leadership. Environmental strategy increasingly sits alongside human capital, education, community investment and governance. EY’s decision to combine these responsibilities gives Leitsch a broader platform to shape how those priorities connect across the firm’s Americas operations.

articles.summary:
Japanese shipping group NYK is moving deeper into Europe’s carbon capture and storage market. The company has agreed to acquire a 30% interest in Norway’s Trudvang CCS project. NYK signed […]
The post NYK Takes 30% Stake in Norway’s Trudvang CCS Project appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
NYK Takes 30% Stake in Norway’s Trudvang CCS Project
- NYK will acquire a 30% interest in Trudvang CCS ANS and the associated Norwegian CO₂ storage exploration license EXL007.
- The investment expands NYK beyond liquefied CO₂ shipping into offshore handling, injection and permanent geological storage.
- Trudvang aims to connect European industrial emitters with offshore CO₂ storage on the Norwegian Continental Shelf.
Japanese shipping group NYK is moving deeper into Europe’s carbon capture and storage market. The company has agreed to acquire a 30% interest in Norway’s Trudvang CCS project.
NYK signed a sale and purchase agreement with Vår Energi CCS AS for a 30% stake in Trudvang CCS ANS. The company will also acquire a corresponding 30% interest in CO₂ storage exploration license EXL007.
The transaction will take place through a wholly owned Norwegian subsidiary that NYK plans to establish. Completion remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.
The deal takes NYK beyond its traditional role as a maritime transport provider. It gives the group direct exposure to offshore CO₂ handling, injection and permanent geological storage.
Building a broader CCS business
NYK has already been developing liquefied CO₂ transportation capabilities through Knutsen NYK Carbon Carriers. The venture is owned equally by NYK and Norway’s Knutsen Group.
That business has focused on the shipping component of the CCS chain. NYK has also been assessing opportunities in related areas, including offshore handling and geological storage.
Trudvang provides a route into those downstream activities.
The company plans to use the project to develop practical expertise in CCS project development. It will also gain experience across the technical and commercial elements of CO₂ transport and storage.
For shipping companies, that diversification could become increasingly important as Europe develops infrastructure to move captured carbon across borders. Industrial emitters may not have suitable storage sites close to their operations. That creates demand for networks capable of transporting CO₂ to permanent offshore storage.
Trudvang targets European industrial emissions
The Trudvang project is being developed under exploration license EXL007 on the Norwegian Continental Shelf.
Its developers aim to establish a transport and storage business for CO₂ captured from European industrial emitters. The system would transport captured carbon for injection into an offshore geological formation and permanent storage.
Technical and commercial studies are currently underway as the partners assess the project’s path toward commercialization.
Vår Energi operates the project, while INPEX Idemitsu Norge AS participates as a partner. Following completion of the transaction, NYK’s Norwegian subsidiary will join the partnership with its 30% interest.
The project reflects a central challenge facing the CCS sector: infrastructure must connect capture facilities with transport networks and viable storage reservoirs.
Without those links, investment in carbon capture at industrial sites can struggle to reach commercial scale.
RELATED ARTICLE: NYK Buys Carbon Removal Credits From Graphyte’s Large Scale Biomass Project
Shipping groups move further into carbon management
NYK intends to apply experience from marine transportation and offshore operations to the project. Its existing activities span areas including exploration and drilling, refining, liquefaction and storage.
That industrial base gives the group a potential route into several parts of the emerging CO₂ logistics market.
Participation in Trudvang will extend its involvement from transportation into offshore handling, injection and storage. It also gives NYK direct experience in a European CCS market shaped by growing industrial decarbonization requirements.
For investors and corporate leaders, the transaction illustrates how CCS is creating business models beyond capture technology itself. Transport infrastructure, offshore operations and storage capacity are becoming distinct parts of the carbon management value chain.
Norway’s role in Europe’s CCS buildout
Norway’s offshore geology and established energy industry have positioned the country as an important prospective storage hub for European captured carbon.
Projects such as Trudvang could support industrial companies that face difficult or costly pathways to eliminate process emissions through electrification or renewable energy alone.
NYK’s entry also shows how established maritime companies can reposition existing capabilities for the low-carbon economy. Shipping expertise becomes particularly relevant when captured CO₂ must move between countries before reaching storage sites.
For NYK, the 30% acquisition creates a foothold beyond transportation. For Europe’s wider CCS market, it adds another shipping and offshore operator to the infrastructure network needed to connect industrial decarbonization plans with permanent carbon storage.

articles.title: NOX Energy Raises $3.4M to Build Europe’s Energy Flexibility Network
articles.summary:
NOX Energy has raised $3.4 million in seed funding to expand software that turns household energy equipment into flexible grid assets. The Belgian startup connects heat pumps and solar panels […]

articles.full_text:
NOX Energy Raises $3.4M to Build Europe’s Energy Flexibility Network
- NOX Energy raised $3.4 million in seed funding to connect household heat pumps and solar systems with European electricity markets.
- The startup says it has connected more than 10,000 devices, as European grids seek flexible capacity to manage growing renewable generation.
- Rise PropTech and Volve Capital co-led the round, following NOX’s $1 million raise in December 2024.
NOX Energy has raised $3.4 million in seed funding to expand software that turns household energy equipment into flexible grid assets.
The Belgian startup connects heat pumps and solar panels with electricity markets. Its technology allows devices to adjust consumption based on electricity prices and grid conditions.
Rise PropTech and Volve Capital co-led the round. Seeder Fund, Uneti Ventures, Fair Capital Impact Fund and 100in also participated.
NOX says it has connected more than 10,000 devices and works with energy suppliers including Eneco and Frank Energie. Its team has grown to 13 people.
“Every time money moves between two banks, it runs over SWIFT. We want to be that for energy flexibility. Millions of homes already have a heat pump, battery or solar panels connected to their manufacturer’s app. Energy suppliers and grid operators need the flexibility these devices can offer, but every manufacturer and every market works differently. NOX sits in between as the infrastructure of flex, connecting both sides. Our goal is for every kilowatt-hour of flexibility in Europe to run through NOX,” said CEO Axelle Moortgat.
Turning homes into flexible grid assets
Europe’s electricity system is becoming increasingly dependent on variable renewable generation.
Wind and solar supplied 30% of EU electricity in 2025, according to Ember. That exceeded fossil fuels, at 29%, for the first time.
Higher renewable penetration increases the value of flexibility. Electricity demand must increasingly respond to periods of abundant or constrained generation.
Homes can provide part of that flexibility without major changes for residents. A heat pump, for example, can pre-heat a property when electricity is cheap. It can then reduce consumption during periods of tighter supply.
NOX connects its software to devices through manufacturers’ or energy suppliers’ existing applications. The platform forecasts a heat pump’s consumption for the following 24 hours and adjusts its operation accordingly.
Grid operators can pay for this flexible capacity. NOX then shares part of that revenue with manufacturers and households.
The company says households can achieve savings of up to 28% and earn up to $225 annually, without installing additional hardware.
Its live integrations cover heat pumps and solar panels. Partners include DeWarmte, NextEnergy, Frank Energie and NIBE Group brands through myUplink.
RELATED ARTICLE: Biden-Harris Invests $40 Million Initiative to Train Clean Energy Workforce
Competition grows around household flexibility
The market is becoming crowded as investors target software capable of coordinating distributed energy resources.
London-based Axle Energy says it manages more than 300,000 devices representing over two gigawatts of flexible capacity. It raised a $25 million Series A led by Energize Capital after earlier seed and pre-seed rounds.
Germany’s 1KOMMA5° raised about $169 million in an extended pre-IPO round in 2025. The company planned to invest more than $112 million in software between 2025 and 2027. Its Heartbeat AI virtual power plant reportedly controls more than 500 megawatts.
Berlin-based Nomos raised about $22.5 million from Index Ventures in September 2026. Its model connects home batteries, electric vehicles and heat pumps to Germany’s electricity market.
Belgian competitor LIFEPOWR raised about $6.4 million in 2025 and manages more than 22,000 connected assets. Companion.energy raised approximately $8.8 million this year, although it focuses on industrial customers.
NOX is positioning itself as a neutral infrastructure layer rather than building a consumer-facing energy supplier. Its current focus remains heat pumps and supplier applications in Belgium and the Netherlands.
Expansion targets Europe’s fragmented flexibility market
The new capital will fund expansion beyond those two markets. NOX also plans deeper integrations with manufacturers and energy suppliers.
The company previously raised about $1 million in December 2024. Its latest round brings disclosed funding to roughly $4.5 million.
For energy companies and investors, the opportunity sits at the intersection of electrification, grid constraints and digital infrastructure. Europe is adding renewable generation while simultaneously electrifying heating and transport.
That creates both pressure and opportunity. Millions of distributed devices could help stabilise electricity systems, but manufacturers, suppliers and grid markets still operate across fragmented technical environments.
NOX is betting that a common software layer can bridge those systems. Its challenge will be achieving scale while larger competitors pursue the same flexible capacity.
If household electrification continues to accelerate, the companies controlling those connections could become an increasingly important part of Europe’s power market infrastructure.

articles.title: FedEx Orders 2,000 Harbinger Electric Trucks in $300 Million Fleet Deal
articles.summary:
FedEx has placed an order for 2,000 all-electric trucks from U.S. manufacturer Harbinger, committing more than $300 million to expand its electric fleet across North America. The vehicles are planned […]
The post FedEx Orders 2,000 Harbinger Electric Trucks in $300 Million Fleet Deal appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
FedEx Orders 2,000 Harbinger Electric Trucks in $300 Million Fleet Deal
- FedEx has ordered 2,000 all-electric medium-duty trucks from Harbinger in a deal valued at more than $300 million.
- The vehicles are planned for delivery by the end of 2027 and will operate across FedEx networks in the United States and Canada.
- Harbinger estimates the fleet could save $800 million in diesel costs and avoid more than 1.7 million tons of CO2 over a 20-year service life.
FedEx has placed an order for 2,000 all-electric trucks from U.S. manufacturer Harbinger, committing more than $300 million to expand its electric fleet across North America.
The vehicles are planned for delivery by the end of 2027. FedEx will deploy them across pickup and delivery operations in the United States and Canada. The trucks will replace conventional vehicles on a one-for-one basis.
The agreement builds on an earlier deployment of Harbinger vehicles within the FedEx network. FedEx also previously co-led Harbinger’s $160 million Series C equity raise.
The companies described the latest transaction as one of the largest binding orders for electric medium or heavy-duty trucks to date.
“FedEx is demonstrating that the business case for incorporating electric vehicles into real-world fleet operations at scale makes sense,” said John Harris, Co-Founder and CEO, Harbinger. “Our previous work together gave FedEx firsthand experience with the performance and economic advantages Harbinger vehicles can deliver. We are proud that a global leader like FedEx is turning its sustainability goals into action by choosing Harbinger to help expand its electric fleet.”
Fleet Economics Move to the Forefront
For large logistics operators, electrification increasingly depends on total operating economics rather than emissions reductions alone.
Harbinger estimates each electric truck can reduce annual fuel costs by an average of $20,000 compared with the diesel vehicle it replaces. Its vehicles are engineered for a 20-year service life, matching the typical lifespan of Class 5 and 6 medium-duty trucks.
Across the 2,000-vehicle order, that could translate into approximately $40 million in annual fuel savings. Harbinger puts cumulative savings at about $800 million over 20 years.
That figure is more than twice the initial value of the vehicle order, although actual savings will depend on factors including mileage, electricity and diesel prices, charging costs and vehicle utilization.
“Electrifying a fleet at this scale requires vehicles that can perform the work our robust operations demand while also delivering meaningful economic benefits,” said Paul Melander, Senior Vice President Safety & Transportation, FedEx and member of Harbinger’s Board of Directors. “Expanding our deployment of Harbinger vehicles gives us an opportunity to continue making progress toward our fleet electrification goals while reducing fuel and operating costs.”
RELATED ARTICLE: FedEx Introduces FedEx® Sustainability Insights in AMEA for Customers Emissions Reporting
Emissions Savings Add to the Business Case
Harbinger estimates replacing 2,000 diesel trucks with its electric models could avoid more than 1.7 million tons of CO2 emissions over their operating lives. The calculation is based on currently published U.S. Department of Energy data.
For FedEx, the order adds another large-scale deployment to its broader fleet modernization efforts. Commercial vehicles are particularly important to transport decarbonization because they can accumulate substantial mileage through predictable operating routes.
Harbinger has also designed its vehicles around daily delivery operations. Features include improved suspension and handling, advanced driver assistance technology and responsive steering. A 42-foot turning diameter is intended to improve maneuverability on dense urban and residential routes.
“The transportation industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation, and electrification is set to play a pivotal role in the future of commercial fleets,” said Vinay D’Souza, Senior Vice President of Global Assets and Infrastructure, FedEx. “This order with Harbinger helps us advance that transition, allowing us to build a more modern, efficient, and intelligent fleet that meets the evolving needs of our customers, our team members, and our global operations.”
What the Deal Means for Commercial Fleet Electrification
The size of the order matters beyond FedEx. Medium-duty trucks occupy a segment where fleet operators can combine emissions reductions with relatively predictable routes, centralized operations and measurable fuel savings.
For investors and corporate leaders, the agreement also illustrates how fleet decarbonization is moving closer to conventional capital allocation decisions. Upfront vehicle costs must increasingly compete against long-term savings in fuel, maintenance and operating expenses.
FedEx’s previous investment in Harbinger adds another dimension. The relationship combines strategic investment, operational testing and now large-scale procurement.
If the projected economics translate into fleet performance, the $300 million-plus order could provide an important commercial reference point for North American electric truck deployment. It also puts long-term operating costs at the center of the case for decarbonizing commercial transport.
